The Budget-Mr. Allard
From the purely constitutional point of view, the Diefenbaker proposals mark a definite progress. The provinces, at least those which insist on their freedom, should find them satisfactory.
A little further down in the same article, Mr. Filion said:
If the provinces wish to get back some of the ground they lost, they must not be content to ask more money from Ottawa but must state their willingness to shoulder heavier responsibilities.
This is what Father Ares, a Jesuit who is an authority on constitutional matters, has to say about the provinces' role in the field of taxation. I am referring to Father Ares' article which appeared in the December 1960 issue of Relations, and more particularly to page 320. I quote:
The provinces must not forget this: if they refuse to make full use of their rights in the taxation field, they forgo the possibility of their becoming modern and independent governments, capable of handling their own destinies and of deciding on their own what policy they should follow; if they refuse to assume the responsibilities freedom entails, they are doomed to mediocrity, they accept their downfall and join the ranks of governments whose subsistence is ensured by a paternalistic and self-seeking metropolitan government. There is but one road open to the provinces if they wish to remain true to their dignity and keep their freedom; they must, right from the start, fully assume their responsibilities in the field of taxation.
I find it difficult, Mr. Speaker, to understand the negative criticism of the Quebec premier, the Hon. Jean Lesage, with respect to the recent proposals made by the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and which take into account the sovereignty and the increasing autonomy of the provinces. Or rather, I can see in what embarrassing position the new premier of Quebec finds himself. At the time he was a member of the federal Liberal government was he not one of those who did the most to hinder provincial autonomy?
May I read here from the speech made by the Hon. Mr. Lesage in this house on April 14, 1954. As seen on page 4078 of Hansard, he said the following:
We cannot, however, accept the unjustified claim that the provinces have priority over the Canadian government in so far as direct taxation is concerned.
And a little further on, he added:
In neither case Mr. Speaker, is there anything but the recognition of a parallel and concurrent right.
So, Mr. Speaker, that was the interpretation that the Hon. Jean Lesage put on the letter and spirit of the confederation pact with a leaning toward centralization and contrary to the interests of the provinces.
But we know that under section 91 of the Canadian constitution, the government of Canada, in the interest of peace, public order

The Budget-Mr. Allard and good administration is entitled to legislate in any matter not included in the classes of subjects assigned exclusively to the provincial legislatures.
Now, in paragraph 2, section 92, of the same constitution, it is provided that the provinces shall have an exclusive right in the matter of direct taxation for provincial purposes. Direct taxation includes personal income tax, succession duties and corporation income tax.
Therefore, the provisions are clear and specific. When provincial purposes are involved, such as education, property and civil rights, the provinces have an exclusive right to direct taxation.
It is not a case, then, as between the federal government and the provinces, of a parallel and joint right to direct taxation for provincial purposes.
Mr. Jean Lesage made in this regard erroneous statements; it is fortunate that our country is now headed by a Progressive Conservative federal government, which is more anxious than he is to preserve those rights and prerogatives our valiant forefathers wrought into the Canadian constitution.
Under the new fiscal formula of the right hon. Prime Minister, the provinces regain possession of their tax fields, enjoy a greater degree of taxation freedom and more of their proper responsibilities.
Before I resume my seat, I would like to suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) a means or method of settlement concerning the important field of education.
Section 93 of the British North America Act says quite clearly that education is the exclusive responsibility of the provinces, except when minority rights are violated in a province.
Also, the courts have decided that the word "education" used in section 93 must have the broadest meaning. A decision of the Supreme Court of Canada reported under "Adoption Act, 1938," page 398 of the report of the supreme court, bears witness to that.
We must therefore progressively eliminate any federal interference in the field of education as experienced in the last century.
I sincerely believe that an integral observance of the constitution is essential for proper political efficiency of the Canadian confederation.
To this effect, I make four suggestions:
1.	That the present government publish its intention to consider as an exclusive provincial responsibility all claims for an in-

crease in the payments made at present by the Canadian government, either to provincial governments, or to educational institutions, as subsidies or any other form of assistance to education, at any level;
2.	That the government adhere to the principle of handing over in due course to the provinces the control and distribution of the various forms of assistance with regard to education, which are now operated by the federal government;
3.	That the solution of this problem be sought by including the present federal payments for education in the equalization payments guaranteed to the provinces under the fiscal agreements, so that both be integrated and considered at the same time when a renewal of the fiscal agreements is discussed;
4.	That this solution be immediately accepted with regard to university grants, it being agreed if necessary that the federal government is willing, until otherwise decided by the fiscal conference, to increase equalization payments each year by the sum representing the intended increase of grants to universities, i.e., by $1.50 per capita of the increased Canadian population.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government would then abstain from paying any additional grants.
A study of the present grant system should be made in order to determine the machinery by which they might be eliminated through their integration with equalization payments.
The amounts voted each year for the Canadian conference of universities would be immediately added to equalization payments and directly handed over to the provinces. It would then be the responsibility of the provinces to make arrangements with the universities to determine the method of distribution, whether through the present Canadian conference of universities, or any other means. It would be the responsibility of the universities themselves to discuss the formula with the provincial governments.
Under such an agreement, no province could claim to be financially wronged by the cancellation of direct grants to the universities. They would receive the same amount, except that they would be free to use it as they pleased. The problem of equalizing the funds available for educational purposes would then be a responsibility of the federal-provincial conference and could be appropriately settled by the parties concerned.

The Budget-Mr. Pitman that government can really be effective. The minister's remarks regarding "bureaucratic delays", and so on, show his idealistic view of so-called laissez-faire, free enterprise school which believes that no government is good government.
The purpose of the budget as expressed by the Minister of Finance is worthy; to solve unemployment, to create a balanced growth in every sector, to improve technical efficiency of industry, to raise the level of savings and investment by Canadians. All of these objectives are very worthy, though we fail to see how this budget is going to accomplish any of these things. We do not believe that government needs to adopt stifling controls; we do believe that a government should provide leadership and planning, something which is completely lacking in this particular government.
What does the minister appeal for throughout the entire budget? He said, as reported at page 6642 of Hansard:
In our free enterprise system we shall need selfdiscipline and the full co-operation of business, labour and all levels of government-
Later in his speech the minister called for "co-operation of labour and management" in regard to prices and wages. In other words, what he expects is foresight and initiative to come from the bottom, when it is completely lacking at the top.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We do not believe the country is on the brink of disaster, as has been claimed. However, we do believe that when a nation has the highest unemployment rate of any developed nation in the world, when it has one of the lowest gross national products of any developed country in the world, when its capital expenditure on plant and factories has gone down to an unbelievably low level, when a small businessman in an area, whether he runs a restaurant, a furniture store or a car lot, finds his profits going down somewhere between 3 to 27 per cent, something seriously needs to be done.
We feel that the tragedy is not so much what is but what could be, in a nation with all the unused plant capacity and unused human resources which the minister spoke about last Tuesday evening. We want to see an expanding economy, and once again we do not see anything in this budget which will give us this.
The minister has said, "We do not intend to let events take an unguided course in the hope that these problems will solve themselves". But that is exactly what happened this last winter. This government would not even admit there was unemployment until some time in December and January. Then

they waited for these problems to solve themselves. This government has no faith in planning. This government cannot plan, because it has no faith in the initiative which would take place if it did.
This budget is concerned entirely with incentive, in the hope that if we spread enough money around at the top, some small part of it will finally find its way and filter down to the bottom. It is completely beyond the comprehension of this government to give money at the bottom and hope that some of it might go to the top.
One of the things this budget is certainly built upon is the hope that the premium on the Canadian dollar will disappear. We want to know by what method. The minister is not suggesting that the foreign exchange board of the second world war is going to be reconstituted and will fix a rate, something that can be depended upon. He suggests, rather, that we are going to set up a foreign exchange fund to buy United States dollars. With an annual average inflow of well over $1 billion, how can one tenth of this create a long term devaluation of the Canadian dollar?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go back to school and find out.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How can the minister be sure that this will not create a considerable fluctuation which will have a very serious effect upon the money market? What of other currencies? I understand that yesterday the relationship of the German mark to the Canadian dollar was exactly the same. In other words someone could have converted Canadian currency to German marks and exchanged German marks into United States currency to escape the premium on the direct conversion. I think this is certainly a problem with which the minister should be concerned.
The minister suggests also that he will lower interest rates. How? I share the concern of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) as to how these rates are going to go down. The minister says he is not going to force the interest rates down.
As he stated-and this appears at page 6645 of Hansard-we attach high importance to a climate of confidence and understanding in our financing matters. Well, all of us have a great deal of confidence in the businessmen of this nation but to expect leadership from them is, I suspect, a matter of misguided hope. Will not the government's needs, with a deficit of $1 billion not raise interest rates, or will the printing presses begin to turn as the hon. member for Trinity suggested? I am all in favour of creating understanding,

but I think this is an area where the government has to take some action and show some initiative.
Certainly, one of the areas where the government is advocating a shrugging off of responsibility is the area of dominion provincial relations. In this respect, the government seems determined to go back to the 1930's. In 1940 this nation had the benefit of having one of the greatest examinations of our federal system which was ever initiated. I will be the first to admit that it was under the Liberal regime. The recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report are, I think, as valid today as they were back in 1940.

speechtext:
That commission thought the solution to our problems would require greater centralization. They thought this was a world wide movement and not simply a matter for Canada to deal with. They believed it was in the interest of all Canadians for the government of Canada to take over certain functions and to take over certain fields of taxation. They believed these policies should be centralized. Equalization, they thought, should be based on a national adjustment grant which would be based on need decided according to expert study. Now, not only is this government determined to excuse its failings by commenting on the confidence of the businessman but it wants to shrug off its responsibilities placing them with the provinces.
The No. 1 weapon by which this government can do anything about unemployment is the monetary and fiscal weapon and now the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is thinking of placing in the hands of the provinces the opportunity to negate whatever the central government is trying to do. A perfect example of this comes right with this budget. Here, this government is going to reduce this tax on automobiles-7A per cent. But what is the premier of the government of Ontario doing? He is putting up the tax by 3 per cent. If the premier of Ontario had pondered for a year to find a way by which he could negate the influence of this government he could not have come up with a better suggestion than a 3 per cent sales tax, the most regressive tax possible. This is an example of what is going to happen. One can see this jungle taking shape in every place in Canada as province after province puts on one tax after another to negate the effect of taxes taken off by the federal government. I think this will be a matter of intense concern to people right across this nation.
Furthermore, once again this equalization is back on a political pandering basis. Forty per cent is given here, $8 million there. The
The Budget-Mr. Pitman government refuses the opportunity to provide leadership and refuses to realize that provincial freedom may involve federal slavery for the Canadian people as a whole.
Perhaps I might give a perfect example of the lack of leadership and direction which has been noticeable in the last six months by drawing attention to one particular problem with which this government tried to deal in the last budget placed before this house. I should like to read from Hansard at page 1007 where the speech is reported in which the Minister of Finance brought forward one of the ways by which the unemployment problem was to be solved. I quote:
The most important of our immediate objectives, as I have already said, is to deal effectively with the problem of unemployment.
I take it, of course, that the minister meant unemployment during this year and not unemployment some years hence. Further on in the same paragraph the hon. gentleman said:
I am anxious to do everything in our means to encourage initiative and enterprise. As a powerful incentive to these ends I am pleased to announce measures to fulfil three major purposes: first, to assist new industries in areas where there is a substantial degree of continuing unemployment over the years-
That was the first proposal. Did this government designate the areas which were to be qualified as surplus manpower areas? No. We heard nothing more about it. When more information did come down, not without considerable prying on the part of the opposition, it came down on March 2. Yet the minister had the audacity to suggest in this budget, and here I read from Hansard at page 6658:
As usual with such matters, interested persons took some time to consider the possibilities in relation to their own affairs and their own plans. Following a time lag which was not unexpected-
The minister went on to say that interest was increasing. The time lag Mr. Speaker was the result of delay by this government. It took until March 2 before any indication was given as to what the criterion might be for those areas which had a surplus manpower. Equivocation of this kind is difficult to stomach. It certainly was not the result of business hesitation. It was because the municipalities did not know whether they were eligible and could not even find out from the government whether they were eligible.
Finally, on March 2, we found out what the criterion was. Was it some glorious, complicated criterion which might have taken months and months of this government's activities to find out? No. It could have been looked up the day after the minister had rushed out his budget speech. It could have been looked up in a chart to be found among
6898	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pitman the documents of the Senate committee on manpower and resources. That criterion could have been announced then. Instead, this government took three months while the unemployment rate was the highest in the history of this nation for the last quarter of a century. This was an inexcusable lack of responsibility. This criterion, again, was combined with another stipulation that the industrial force must be going down. That is when the Department of Labour or the Department of Finance, through its officials, should have been in these constituencies finding out whether or not the employment force had gone down. I am not, of course, suggesting that what was being offered to these areas of surplus manpower would be any use whatsoever-double depreciation for one year is practically useless. In fact, I would ask this question: how many industries are, six months later, receiving the benefit of this allowance? I would be very interested to know, because this is one of the most fantastic negations of government responsibility that I have ever seen.

It took four months from the bringing down of the last budget before one area had been designated, namely, Cornwall. It took from March 21 to May 4 for the government to figure out that Windsor should be designated as such an area. Then-this is the greatest joke of all-a few days ago they had to change the rules so that they could bring in the one area which they were trying to get in, namely, Elliot Lake. The government had refused to tell the areas which had an opportunity to come under this scheme whether they were eligible or not. But I have worked out-and I can assure hon. members it did not take me long-a list of the major industrial areas of 10,000 people and more who have the required 75 per cent of unemployment and, as of June 2, Shawinigan Falls, which had 90.5 per cent, had not applied; Grand Val d'Or had not applied; Cornwall had applied and been accepted; Lac St. Jean with 32.6 per cent had not applied; Trois Rivieres with 90.5 per cent had not applied, Brantford, with 90.5 per cent had not applied -had not even been told that they were in a category where they could apply. So what do we have? As of June 2 there was 39 places which had applied and most of them, well over 50 per cent of them, are way below what has been set out in this particular criterion. They have no chance of gaining any help whatsoever from the scheme which has been designated by this government.
I know of one case where the municipal council of a city tramped all the way down here to Ottawa and spent the day down here, the taxpayers' money having been spent on


sending them down here, to spend a couple of hours with a minister of the crown to find out where they belonged in this category. They could have been told that they belonged in that category by means of a phone call in two minutes. It took me 15 minutes to find out what the percentage was by simply looking through the copies of the Labour Gazette which are to be found in the library of this particular house. That is an instance of the lack of responsibility, the lack of leadership, the lack of initiative with which this government has conducted its affairs over the past six months. We are presented with a huge deficit and told by the Minister of Finance that this will not cause any real inflation. He then adds that modest price advances in regard to some of the goods we obtain from abroad as well as in regard to some of our export commodities will occur. What consideration does he give to the consumer or those individuals who are on pensions and whose incomes are stabilized, those individuals who are so dependent on welfare benefits? I suggest there is not a bit of concern given to those people. It's a budget of bits and pieces.
I should like to read from page 5 of the report from the Senate special committee on manpower and employment as follows:
The maintenance of an adequate rate of economic growth requires a continuing high level of capital investment, both private and public. Private capital investment must be supplemented and stimulated by an adequate rate of government investment in social capital.
This is an area which the present budget has missed completely. The report then continues as follows:
Our stock of social capital is both inadequate and in many respects obsolescent, especially in our rapidly expanding urban areas.
Has this government dealt with anything in that area? I suggest it has not. That certainly indicates poverty of imagination and a complete lack of a recognition of the major problem of this nation.
This huge deficit is being used as an answer to the problem in a manner similar to spreading out a mass of green and white bottles on the floor and then turning a firehose on the bottles with the expectation that some water will go into the green bottles but none into the white bottles.
There is no indication in this budget as to the determining of whether this huge deficit and the money resulting from it will be directed into those areas where it will provide employment. I suggest it sets forth a firehose approach which I am convinced will have very little effect upon the problems of this nature.

The minister is determined that he is going to increase the investment in Canada by Canadians. Here again there is no plan for creating some kind of Canadian development fund to provide incentive and encouragement to Canadians to invest their money in areas where it is socially desirable, none whatsoever. Once again the incentive is provided at the top with the hope that some of it will drop to the bottom. Again, is this not a time for lower taxes in certain areas so as to provide greater employment?
We note with satisfaction that the minister is now determined to do something about the individuals with high expense accounts; expense account living, he called it. His answer to this problem is simply that the Department of National Revenue will scrutinize this type of thing. I suggest this is not enough.
In conclusion I should like to state that this is the last time that the C.C.F. party as such will have the opportunity of discussing a budget on the floor of this house. For that reason, and in view of the budget which has been brought down, I feel that a few facts placed on the record might be of value.
Family allowance payments this year will be $523 million. Old age assistance payments, blind persons and disabled persons' allowances and unemployment assistance will be in the amount of $96,856,000. Hospital insurance and general health grants will amount to $317 million. Old age security payments -expenditures from the old age security fund -will amount to $606,570,000.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to participate in a budget debate, and I must compliment the minister and the government for this budget which, in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of many other Canadians, is a good budget.
I was very interested on Tuesday evening last to hear the remarks of Dr. Hannam, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, who said that in his opinion this budget would do much of benefit to agriculture in Canada.
I wish to deal with three matters which I feel are of urgent importance. The first is of regional concern, but, in my opinion, of national importance. Since 1950 in Canada and particularly in western Canada we have built up a beef industry with the largest market being the United States. Over the past years farmers' incomes have been increased in part as a result of the shipment of dressed and live beef to the United States. In western Canada this year the farmers are facing a drought situation.
I should just like to refer to the latest issue of the Manitoba Co-Operator dated June 15. In that issue under the heading "Drought and Livestock" there appears the statement that Manitoba's pasture and hay picture this season to date has not been as grim since the 1930's. This same situation applies to all three western provinces where there will be no early hay cut this year. Normally the first cut of hay should have already been taken, but this year farmers will be fortunate to take one crop in July or early August.
Since this government came into office in 1957 it has recognized Canada's agricultural industry as it has never been recognized by any previous government. This government has placed legislation on the statute books of great benefit to Canada's agricultural industry
6900	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Speakman across the nation, and has increased the level of income and standard of living of those individuals participating in this industry; although not to the degree desired, this is a step in the right direction.
Among the pieces of legislation which this government has enacted is the measure providing the acreage payments made in 1958 and again in 1960 on the basis of emergency. I should like to state that in my opinion the present situation in western Canada constitutes another similar emergency. One of our major sources of United States dollars exists through the export of beef to the United States. I suggest that if the beef farmers are not assisted in the provision of funds to purchase fodder for their beef herds these herds will have to be drastically reduced with a resultant loss in economy, both regional and national, for some considerable time. I suggest the situation has never been as bad since the 1930's as far as drought is concerned as it is now, when we are just nicely recovering from the losses suffered from the outbreak of hoof and mouth disease in 1950. We have our herds back; we have a good market and I would hope that the government would seriously consider paying the $1 an acre again this year.
The second matter that I should like to deal with is one that I consider to be in the national interest. It is in the interest of all of Canada from the point of view of employment, and from the point of view of a balance of payments with the United States, and it is in the interest of Canadian development and national advancement. I want to speak for a few moments on the Canadian case for the Montreal pipe line.
In the area east of the Ottawa valley we have the largest concentration of users of the products of our oil industry being supplied at the present time almost wholly by foreign imports. In effect this situation is creating employment outside of Canada when we need so much an increase in employment in Canada.
Recently a booklet was put out by Home Oil Company Limited of Canada, and I should like to refer, if I may, to one or two sections of it. The booklet is called "The Canadian Case for the Montreal Pipe Line". They begin by saying:
The Montreal pipe line project, must succeed or fail on whether it serves the national interest of Canada.
In my opinion it has failed to do so. I continue:
The proposal to construct a $430 million large diameter pipe line to Montreal falls four-square within the national interest as so defined.

Our productive capacity of crude oil, sir, is 1,100,000 barrels of oil a day. At the time this booklet was printed we were producing 525,000 barrels a day and importing more than 410,000 barrels of crude oil products a day from outside the country. I continue:
The building of a Montreal pipe line, and the consequent utilization of western Canadian crude oil, can reduce Canada's merchandise trade deficit by more than $200 million in 1963, increasing to more than $400 million per year by 1972.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is a worth-while objective for Canadians. The booklet goes on:
The building of a large diameter crude oil pipe line from Alberta to Montreal will provide direct employment for 6,000 Canadians and indirect employment for more than an additional 25,000 during the two-year construction period.
The pipe line will require approximately 700,000 tons of steel, all of which can be produced from Canadian iron ore and fabricated in Canada into 2,100 miles of Canadian pipe.
There again we would create additional employment. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians would gladly pay perhaps a little more for their oil products which they require and use, in the interest of providing employment for other Canadians, rather than providing employment for people in outside countries.
In addition, the building of this pipe line would give a great impetus to national development, to the expansion which the minister and the government so desire. Our known potential of crude oil is more than 30 years' supply for Canadians and our expected potential is probably something like 300 years' supply. Therefore, I believe we would be better off as Canadians to use our own product and develop our own oil rather than give this employment, as I said before, to people outside of Canada.
The third subject that I should like to deal with I like to think is global. As all hon. members know, I had the honour and the privilege in April and May of this year to attend as Canada's delegate the meeting of parliamentarians from the nations and dependencies of the commonwealth, which was held at the houses of parliament in London, England, and at Stormont, the parliament of Northern Ireland. It was a great privilege for me to attend this conference, sir. Before I go any further I should like to urge the government to consider very seriously increasing by a very large amount its contribution to the Canada branch of the commonwealth parliamentary association so that more members of the Canadian House of Commons and of the other place might be able to visit the countries of the commonwealth.
It was very interesting indeed to find, when we were assembled in the houses of parliament in London, that of the 32 delegates

three were white. I think this provides a very interesting commentary on the position of the white people in the world today. In fact their position is perhaps not quite as ascendant as it was. There were 12 delegates from the various nations in Africa; four from commonwealth countries in the Orient; three from India; seven were of Arabian nationality and three from the West Indies. I was delighted indeed to find that all of these people from all of these countries held Canada and Canada's Prime Minister in the highest respect. In fact, the remark made by many of them was that they consider the Prime Minister of Canada to be the foremost figure on the political scene in the world today.
During the passage of another piece of legislation in the house this week, Mr. Speaker, I made mention of the needs of some of these member nations of the commonwealth in respect of the things which we in Canada can provide. I was amazed to read in a report of one of the committees of the house that one of my colleagues had suggested the government should reduce its aid to African nations. In my opinion, sir, we should vastly increase aid to Africa particularly. There is a need for advancement in agriculture. They are farming under very primitive conditions. They have no other source of national income, really. In most African countries their young men and women have to leave home to make a living. Canada could make a tremendous contribution, sir, to the advancement of those nations and by making this contribution it could certainly help to weld this commonwealth into what it could be.
I should like to see my colleagues in all parts of the house support such a move to extend this assistance to those African nations; in fact, to all of the commonwealth nations. I would hope that it would be done soon. It is my opinion that the commonwealth, rather than any other organization in the world today, provides us with our greatest hope for world peace and security. With the commonwealth we can weld together and keep together a team whose members are multiracial and speak many languages but with a common devotion to the crown and the common bond that most of the people in these countries can speak the English language. I would hope that we in Canada would adopt an attitude as a nation and as a people not of what can we get but what can we give in today's world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget brought down two nights ago aroused a great deal of interest. There was perhaps more interest this year than at any time in the recent past. There was much anticipation and much
The Budget-Mr. Granger speculation because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had indicated that he was going to produce an expansionist budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The word "expansionist" had a magical effect. Canada, still in a period of recession, still plagued with unemployment, was really in difficulties. There was no official admission that the nation was in trouble but there was a sort of unofficial acknowledgement that all was not well and among the public there was concern that this condition of recession might not cure itself.
The announcement of an expansionist budget was welcomed generally and excitement ran high. Certainly there is reason to call the budget the great expectations budget. Tuesday night came and the great expectations budget was brought down. The preamble was heroic and heroically delivered. The minister's words were optimistic. He said, as found on page 6641 of Hansard:
The normal growth of real demand can be expected to overtake capacity in the not too distant future.
A great part of the budget speech was an attempt to explain the new policies which were about to be produced, policies which it was indicated would make Canada a land flowing with milk and honey and bursting with prosperity. The minister admitted as he proceeded with his speech that all was not well. This was a new departure, one of several in what was in fact an unusual budget. He had this to say in his speech:
There is more unemployment and unused capacity in our industries than we can possibly accept. Recent rates of economic growth have been lower than we need to absorb our rapidly growing labour force and the output of our expanding industrial capacity.
This was a very neat way of formally acknowledging that there has been an unemployment problem. A little later he used another neat phrase when he said, as found on page 6642 of Hansard:
We do not intend to let events take an unguided course-
One must note, however, that he did not announce a planned economy. One statement he made was soon proven to be correct, namely:
The budget which I bring down this evening is not an ordinary budget.
It certainly was not an ordinary budget. It was not set in the usual ideological background either. This was to be an expansionist budget, not one of the ordinary run of the mill, pay as you go budgets. The passing of the years and the persistence of economic troubles had induced a change of thinking if not a change of heart.

The Budget-Mr. Granger
Deficits are not new to this government There were deficits in 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961 and a huge deficit is expected and planned for in 1962. I might also go so far as to say that deficits are a way of life with the present administration. However, to embrace deficit financing as a way to prosperity and to hail it as a noble means to a glorious end is a new philosophy for this administration.
I hasten to add that deficit financing is not necessarily bad or perhaps I should say that deficit financing can be justified. I am not criticizing the decision to resort to deficit financing. I am merely wondering at the complete change in economic philosophy which accompanied its announcement. In a time of economic stress and strain there is positive justification for resorting to deficit financing provided that the deficit financing is to create something new. However, it appears to me that all the present deficit does is to cause us to go deeper into debt in order to pay off old debts. The present deficit financing seems to have been forced on the government rather than having been sought out to create a better and healthier economic state.
Then there is the matter of delay in introducing the budget, for there was an inordinate delay in introducing the budget this year. The budget is, I suppose, about three months late. The delay has caused great anxiety, concern and uncertainty in the Canadian business community. The only possible justification for such a delay would have been the presentation of a far-reaching budget introducing major changes, but there are really no major changes in the budget. To my way of thinking, it is not a document which would justify such a delay and the resultant consequences of the delay that have occurred upon Canadian business. The conclusion which the Canadian public must reach with regard to the delay is that it represents both the arrogance and the poor administration of the government.
The only substantial measure introduced by the government is the use of the exchange fund to attempt to influence the external value of the Canadian dollar. This fund has existed for at least 20 years. It now stands, I believe, at nearly $2 billion. The government could have employed this fund at any time to influence the exchange rate. It did not require a budget to enable the government to use this fund. The fact that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to emphasize the use of the exchange fund and calls this a major measure shows the lack of dynamic ideas in the budget. The use of the exchange fund is rather like finding an old toy in the closet, bringing it out and polishing it up and becoming excited over it. Too little and too late

may well apply to this budget of great expectations. It is questionable if the budget contains the power, the real power to bring about the upward change and the rise in industrial development which it forecast. There is wind without the windmill. There are great promises which require real geared energy in order to fulfil them. The substance is not there. Of course, time will prove the value of all the prophecies which have been made.
However, I cannot help but think back to some of the great national projects which were initiated under the previous Liberal administration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose I was recalling some of the great national projects which had been initiated under previous Liberal administrations. I would mention among others the Trans-Canada Air Lines, the trans-Canada highway, the trans-Canada pipe line and the St. Lawrence seaway. I cannot help but deplore the fact that there does not seem to be provision made in this budget for the development of further great national projects in the near future. I might add that such national projects serve a twofold purpose; they give a boost to the national economy and they develop the cohesion and maturity of Canada as a nation.
It is a matter of regret that there are no great new national projects forecast at the present time because such national projects would more than justify a deficit. The only expansion on the horizon in an expansion of debt without the compensation of expanded productivity.
I should like to make some reference to parts of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance which were devoted to international trade and commercial policies. The minister seemed to reject most of the views of people who have been thinking about Canada's trading problems. I think he referred to them as "counsels of fear and even despair".
The point which I wish to emphasize is that all the discussion regarding the need for fundamental rethinking in Canada's trading position, and the many arguments that have been presented, notably those by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) regarding the need for Canada to recognize and assess the impact of European trade developments, have apparently been rejected as well as the proposal put forward regarding new horizons for Canada's trade. The minister said:
I do not believe that the economic problems which confront Canada today require a drastic redirection of our trading relationships; or that these problems cannot be overcome by a vigorous pursuit of our present trading policies judiciously adjusted to meet changing world conditions.
The Budget-Mr. Allmark
The minister made some reference to the prospect of Britain entering the European common market and it seemed to me that he did not think Britain should join that group. On the other hand, it seemed to me that the tenor of his remarks held implications that Britain would be doing Canada a disservice if she joined that common market. If I am right in my assumption that the Canadian government is opposed to Britain entering the European market, I should like to ask what alternative policy or proposal the Canadian government has to offer the British government.
If Britain considers that it is essential to her economy to join the European common market, we should act constructively so that Britain and Canada can strengthen their economies and expand their trade. I suggest the time has come for Canada to show a greater long term understanding of the position of the British government and to attempt to make arrangements whereby she can share the increased prosperity which this move could bring to Britain, to the common market and to the commonwealth.
I believe there is no more important area in which new thinking is required in Canada than in respect to our trading relationship with Britain and the European trade bloc. The Minister of Finance seemed to be neglecting the opportunity which exists to expand our future trading prospects in these areas of the world, and I should like to suggest that he spend some time studying the arguments put forward in this house time and time again by the Leader of the Opposition and others regarding the Atlantic economic community.
The budget of great expectations is already petering out in uneasiness and disappointment. I think it would be unfair to blame all this on the Minister of Finance who, after all, is in the rather unenviable position of operating a cash register in which there is no cash. It was the Prime Minister who, in 1958, sowed the wind and it is now the people of Canada who are reaping the whirlwind. The long delay in the so-called expansionist budget has become, in the words of the Leader of the Opposition, an expansion of wind, word and debt.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations, to those already expressed, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for his very able presentation of the budget. May I say that in this presentation the minister has again shown that quality of good judgment he has always exhibited since first occupying this portfolio.

The Budget-Mr. Allmark
The budget debate provides an excellent opportunity tor members who are backbenchers to pass along to parliament the advice and opinions of those whom they represent in their ridings. I would like to commend the ministers on their readiness to turn a sympathetic ear to the problems of the private members and since this receptive attitude exists on their part I should like to take this opportunity to pass along to hon. members on the front benches the comments, praise and criticism of those who live in both the urban and the rural sections of my historic riding.
One of the most frequent complaints concerns the unemployment insurance fund. I know that all Canadians are anxious to help those who are in need but I do think there are areas where we could do more than we are doing at the present time. May I say that many of my constituents are not at all satisfied with the hand-out of insurance funds to those who are not in need. I am sure that the public is not opposed to married women drawing unemployment insurance if it is necessary for them to supplement the income going into their homes, but there are, I find, many who are definitely opposed to married women drawing unemployment insurance when their husbands are taking home $4,000 or $5,000 a year. We know there are thousands in Canada who are doing this and we do not have to look very far for examples of such misuse of the insurance fund.
Possibly because I come from a port on the great lakes I have always supported the Canadian sailor. I have stated on a good number of occasions that as pilots and ship handlers Canadian sailors have no equal. They work hard in the job which has its disadvantages and discomforts. They deserve good pay. But 1 see no justification for sailors who are making between $5,000 and $10,000 a year receiving unemployment insurance during the winter months. I have friends who are in the top salary bracket and who enjoy the luxury of having their unemployment insurance cheques mailed to them in the winter months. These men are good Canadians; I am sure they do not believe that this is the purpose of the fund. But one cannot expect them to refuse what is lawfully and cheerfully provided.
I have the opportunity which all hon. members do to help many elderly people in my riding. There are many Canadians who do not have an opportunity fully to realize the tremendous blessing which the old age pension is to elderly people. There is, however, an area to which further consideration should be given. There are cases where the survivor of a couple who have made ends meet on both


old age pensions finds great difficulty in managing on a single pension. Sometimes extreme hardship has to be faced. It has been my privilege in many cases to assist such people to obtain supplementary assistance from the province and from the municipality. However, in such cases an investigation is made as to means and this adds to the upset state which bereavement has already brought to these people. I would strongly recommend that some method be found to increase the income of such persons without making it necessary for them to appeal to charitable organizations.
The residents of my constituency are extremely grateful for the assistance given by this government to the shipbuilding industry. We are aware that in the shipbuilding trade in recent years and particularly since the opening of the seaway competition from foreign countries has been very keen. Had this provision for assistance not been made we were faced with the loss of those skills which are peculiar to this trade and which would be almost impossible to replace. Thus we were faced with the loss of an important Canadian industry. May I remind the government that there will no doubt be considerable work to be done in the conversion of the best of the old canal ships to a larger and more economic size for use in the new canal and I would ask that consideration be given to the application of this subsidy to the conversion of existing Canadian ships.
No one who has followed the shipbuilding industry has failed to notice the number of times foreign engines are used in ships belonging to the Canadian government. Too frequently we find that these ships are designed so that Canadian marine engines cannot be adapted for use in them, or that they can be adapted only at considerable additional cost. I believe that when it is decided that the Canadian government needs new ships there should be a consultation at the; design stage with a committee of government to ensure that the ship was not so designed as to exclude the use of Canadian machinery and equipment. We have in Canada two marine engine manufacturers. One of them is a Kingston plant. The marine engines produced by these Canadian companies are at least equal to those produced by any country and it is shocking to find that on occasions we appear to give preference to engines and equipment produced by other countries. If we believe the "Buy Canadian" slogan, let us make sure that our government ship designers do not prevent us from practising this policy.
Until recent years in my historic riding we were very proud of our transportation

system both by water and and by rail. Kingston is on the main line of the Toronto-Mont-real route of the railway. Our passenger and freight service by rail was equal to the best in Canada. Our passenger and freight service by water was also equal to the best in Canada because we were one of the important ports on the St. Lawrence-great lakes system. Ninety per cent of all the ships which passed from river to lake or down from lake to river passed the port of Kingston. But the shipping channel, either through stupidity or design was diverted, under the previous government, to the United States side, missing the port of Kingston. In addition, under former governments, when the necessity for air service became apparent, only a few feeble attempts were made to provide my constituency with this modern system of travel. It is said that the wheels of government turn slowly. But may I say that it is only a little more than three years since the people of Canada elected a government of Sir John A's party and in this short period of time a contract has been awarded which in its first step will provide a connection with the seaway channel to the east. This will permit 90 per cent of the present seaway vessels to use the Canadian side and to pass the port of Kingston. Also in this short period of time the government has studied and realized the need for air service and has granted a licence under which Kingston will have a daily air service to Toronto and Montreal, commencing at the end of this month. I should like very sincerely to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) for their interest, their sound judgment and their progressiveness in bringing those services to my riding. At this time I should like to say how much I appreciate the assistance of our local council and the businessmen of my riding who took the time to come to Ottawa and efficiently present briefs supporting those necessary services.
At the junction of the St. Lawrence and lake Ontario, where the city of Kingston is situated, there are a number of very beautiful islands. Two of those are large and have a large population of year round residents in addition to those hundreds of people who have their summer homes there. The great problem for those who make their homes on the islands is transportation to the mainland, particularly at the time of freeze-up and at the spring break-up. To cross over the ice in the spring and fall is very hazardous and through the years there has been a tragic loss of life.
There is only one proper solution to this problem, Mr. Speaker, and that is the building of a bridge to span the distance from
The Budget-Mr. Allmark the mainland to Howe island, thence to Wolfe island and from there to the United States mainland. Unfortunately, the bankers who finance such projects as international bridges assess only the financial returns and attach no importance to the great benefit to those who must make this hazardous crossing in the spring and fall, nor does the loss of life enter into their calculations.
This project has been studied by committees on both the United States and Canadian sides of the river, and, while all agree on the great benefits a bridge would bring to the area, there is also agreement that such a project is impossible without government assistance. May I suggest to the Minister of Public Works that his very capable economic study group under the leadership of Dr. Weeks might well look at this proposal with a view to assessing the benefits which would accrue not only to those who live on the islands but also to the entire area through increased tourist traffic. It does seem to me that here is an excellent opportunity for the government to be of service to Canadians which would result in a tremendous benefit in the development of the area and, what of course is more important, it would save human life.
In the rural area surrounding the city of Kingston the chief occupation of those who are engaged in farming is the dairy industry. We realize that this government has been particularly interested in the welfare of the farmers, and particularly aware that the dairy industry is one which has not received a fair return for its production. While the farmers in my area appreciate the legislation which has been passed by the Conservative government to stabilize farm prices, I should like to impress upon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) the fact that the dairy industry is likely to continue to have a problem and it is our responsibility to continue to study and improve the conditions in this industry which is so vital to our country.
We in the riding of Kingston are grateful to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) for the granting of an additional $100,000 toward the cost of Kingston's sewage disposal program. We also commend the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) for the extension of mail carrier service to the residential areas which lie outside our city.
We are grateful to the Minister of Public Works for his co-operation with Canada Steamship Lines and James Richardson Company in dredging Little Cataraqui bay so as to provide a deep water port for the city of Kingston.
As I mentioned earlier, we are extremely grateful for our air service and the connecting

The Budget-Mr, Allmark channel to the seaway. May I, however, remind the Minister of Public Works, who I know has some very close ties with my riding, that he may expect me back in his office shortly urging further port improvements so that the port of Kingston may share in the development of this promising area.
Before coming to the House of Commons I was an employee of a Canadian industry with an excellent pension scheme. However, Canadian workers are aware that even the best of our Canadian pensions have one great weakness; they are not portable. Industrial employees in my riding have discussed this matter of the portability of pensions with me on numerous occasions and I should like to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that his statement during the presentation of the budget that steps will be taken to deal with this matter will be indeed welcome news to Canadian workers.
In closing I should like to mention a subject which is important to my own riding and the surrounding ridings. While I have admiration for the qualities of the man whose empire I propose to bring to the attention of this parliament, I think it proper that I should level criticism because of the great concern expressed to me by residents of my constituency. I refer to the control of the news media over a wide area of eastern Ontario which is held by one man. Not only does he control the news media in my riding but also in adjoining ridings. Let me be specific. There is one daily newspaper in Kingston and one in Peterborough. This man owns both. There is one T.V. station in each of those ridings. He controls both. There are four radio stations in the two ridings, and of those he controls two. Licences for both the T.V. and the radio stations were granted to this Liberal Senator by the previous Liberal government. This man, whose newspapers pose as being politically independent, had this to say in a speech to the commonwealth press union, reported in the Ottawa Journal of June 15 of last year. I quote:
The new government has appointed a hoard of broadcast governors which has proved to be very autocratic. This board tells stations what to do and what not to do. How much time to devote to each item. How much profit must be devoted to the development of local talent. Some of us are worried that this might eventually affect the freedom of newspapers.
Here is a man who has gained control of the news media over a large area who is obviously concerned only that this government should not disturb his empire. I believe it is utterly impossible to have freedom of the press, or to have an informed public, when almost 100 per cent of the control of the news media over a large area is held by one man. It is in my opinion impossible for


any person to have such a monopoly of the news, such a power to influence people's minds, without using it for his own personal advantage. Frankly, I see little difference between the government controlled press such as exists in some countries and a news monopoly held by one person such as we have in this instance. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is the responsibility of the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. to take such steps as are necessary to break up these monopolies wherever they may exist across Canada.
