subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Tuesday night's budget was introduced under very unusual circumstances. Never had a rendering of accounts to the country been delayed so long. The most surprising thing is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) did not attempt to give an explanation or a reason to justify such a delay.
Therefore, the government is responsible for the confusion and uncertainty in which business and industry in general have found themselves since the end of last March, the time when a diligent government usually gives an account of its administration.
The four previous budgets submitted by the present government showed substantial deficits. At times the economy was at a standstill, according to the government, at other times we had come out of a momentary recession, but never in those four years had the Canadian citizen the clear impression that their government was aware of the actual problems and shortcomings of our economy and took appropriate action to correct them.
Last year, for instance, on the basis of a 6 per cent rise in gross national income, the Minister of Finance forecast a surplus of approximately $13 million; yet, last December, we heard that that surplus was to become a deficit of about $350 million because gross national income had not met the minister's hopes.
The Minister of Finance who has already been nicknamed "Donald deficit" by some people, has become our national "Wrong way Corrigan" with his record-breaking deficit of $1 billion forecast for the current year.
That means, that after five and a half years of Conservative administration, this country is $2.5 billion deeper in the red. I am not against deficits as such, because they are sometimes necessary.
I think Canadians, in general, were expecting an expansionist and therefore adverse budget. However, like most of my fellow-citizens, I am deceived because, if it is true

that we will have a deficit at the end of the next fiscal year, we are far from being sure that the program introduced by the Minister of Finance will bring us the expansion he promised.
The Conservative party still bears the mark of Toryism, and in this situation into which we were thrown by this administration I submit that the Liberal expansionist program would have been a hundred times better.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What program?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must reply to my hon. friend who just interrupted me, that we have submitted a program under which a national tax reduction would have brought immediate dividends to every class of citizens.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and my hon. friends should be reminded here that the working class like others, the humble class, the class of small wage-earners should have been directly considered and protected under this so-called expansionist program, which in fact is mostly based on artificial measures.
This budget is not a budget for the majority of our people who shall still have to be content with a few crumbs that may fall from the table of the wealthy.
The disastrous results achieved so far by the Minister of Finance force us to accept his predictions under beneficium inventorii and I feel that an editorial of the Ottawa Citizen of June 21 expressed quite accurately my views in that regard.
(Text):
Mr. Fleming's past performances as a prognosticator being what they are, it is difficult to feel anything but the most profound uneasiness as he offers his new prescription for an ailing economy. The Minister of Finance sounds his usual ringing note of confidence, but the fact remains that he is embarking on a gigantic gamble. It carries the danger if not the outright guarantee of inflation. In this budget, Mr. Fleming frankly goes out to achieve a deficit of some $650 million. This assumes an increase in revenues between now and next March 31 as a result of the stimuli being applied to Canadian business. In any event, the accumulated deficits of the present government promise to top the $2 billion mark before it has been five years in office, which is quite a feat.
Part of the minister's objective is to bring down interest rates. How he expects to do this in the face of such monumental deficit financing, with its consequent effect on the money market, is difficult to see.
(Translation):
And the article concludes as follows: (Text):
Yet while these features of the budget appear satisfactory as far as they go, the document as a whole is a disturbing one. It is overshadowed by yet another deficit, and while a case may be made out for deficits for pump-priming purposes, Mr. Fleming has become addicted to them as to a drug. It remains to be seen how the business and financial community reacts to the latest in the series. Any
The Budget-Mr. Deschatelets outcome of the experiment in manipulation of the exchange fund is unpredictable. Pushing buttons without knowing just what will happen is a risky game.
Canadians will hope that the minister's gamble will turn out all right. It will be unfortunate for the country as well as for the government if it does not.
(Translation):
Everyone is aware of the well-known unbiased and objective attitude of the Ottawa Citizen.
Mr. Speaker, following even a superficial examination of the budget, you cannot but reach the conclusion that the Conservative government has been faithful to its past and its Tory spirit.
While radical measures are imperative, we only get words and wind; while a measure of tax reduction is offered, there is nothing for the small wage-earner, nothing for the working classes, nothing for the unemployed, except perhaps renewed concern about the presits tory spirit.
The small wage-earner will be the first to bear the brunt of the budget. It is he, in fact, who will have to shoulder the burden of that budget.
As I said earlier, the economy is not like a car. A car can be shifted into gear, its speed can be increased by pressing on the gas, and it can be stopped by applying the brakes.
You cannot do that with a country's economy.
You will also recall the government's lack of judgment in trying to divert to the United Kingdom 15 per cent of our trade with the United States. You will also recall the difficulties that followed that irresponsible statement.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to that new policy announced by the Minister of Finance Tuesday, concerning the exchange rate control. That is one of the main points in the budget.
With that policy, the government hopes to control the exchange rate, even to reduce it, through the exchange fund.
But a report published in La Presse of June 21, sets forth a very interesting opinion in that connection:
The minister proposes to reduce the exchange rate.
And the minister goes on:
More than any other policy that could be adopted, a lower exchange rate will be of signal assistance to all of our producers, both in primary and in secondary industries, to those who export as well as to those who sell at home.
There had also been a rather interesting article concerning the budget brought down on March 31, 1960. The Minister of Finance had then made a statement on the same subject in utter opposition to this one.

The Budget-Mr. Deschatelets
I quote:
I have seen some references to a demand that the government should deliberately "devalue" the dollar. This kind of talk might have been appropriate when Canada was on the gold standard, or even when it maintained a fixed exchange rate. We have not been on the gold standard for half a century and we have not had a fixed exchange for a decade. An attempt by the government, added Mr. Fleming, artificially to lower the external price of the Canadian dollar would involve sums of money with which to buy up foreign exchange.
The minister added:
It would be a very difficult matter to work out technical controls.
In other words, we would be embarking upon a gigantic financial speculation with no assurance of success.
I have just shown that this new policy is a complete reversal of the minister's former position concerning the exchange rate.
And yet that was what the minister said on March 30 last.
I cannot understand why the minister is saying exactly the opposite of what he was stating last year. I wonder when he is speaking the truth. Was it last year, when he said that the artificial reduction of the exchange rate was bad policy. Or is it this year, when he says that it is sound policy. I must tell the minister that there are a thousand ways of controlling the exchange rate, but there is a way that could prove very bad because of unforeseen consequences, and that way is precisely this artificial method adopted by the government Tuesday night.
Canada is an exporting nation. We must therefore take that into account and adjust our economy in such a way as to achieve commercial expansion and competitive prices on world markets. One must not forget however that we are equally dependent on. a great many imported products for our very subsistence. I will mention the most essential ones, those which may be found on every Canadian table: tea, coffee, sugar, etc.
As a result of this change in the rate, our Canadian families should necessarily expect to pay more for imported products. I should like to ask the minister what provisions there are in his budget against such an occurrence? What will happen to the lower and middle classes if there is a sharp rise in the cost of living?
I know of experts who have expressed the opinion that the cost of living index could go up by as much as five points. Regarding this matter I should like to read a most interesting article which appeared in this morning's Gazette, that is the June 22 issue, under the signature of Mr. John Meyer. It is entitled:


(Text):
The full cost of budget has still to be figured.
Mr. Fleming will have to borrow an average of $100 million a month for the balance of the fiscal year to meet his estimated cash deficit. No provision was made for the $100 million needed for the debt management fund. There will probably be other non-budgetary expenditures which haven't yet been accounted for. The heaviest cost is likely to arise from keeping the dollar at a discount. A total borrowing half again larger than that indicated remains a distinct possibility. Meeting this requirement and, at the same time, reducing interest rates will be a remarkable accomplishment to bring about without inflating the money supply.
(Translation):
Now, I ask the minister: how much will the government have to borrow monthly in order to meet the requirements of its deficits? What will happen to the interest rates which the government is anxious to maintain at a reasonable level? What are the means provided in this budget to maintain those interest rates at a reasonable level? What will happen to the loans of our provincial governments, of our municipalities, past loans as well as future loans?
Shall we be in a position to meet their needs if they are unable to obtain funds on foreign markets, as far as financing is concerned? I am thinking in particular of the Montreal subway project, about which it was reported that financial arrangements were almost completed with the French government, because at that time, Canadian businessmen had been extremely surprised and taken aback when they heard that the Canadian government was unable to supply funds to our own municipalities, which were forced to borrow on foreign markets.
Well, today, with the adoption of those measures, I submit that such financing will place the provinces and municipalities in a very difficult situation, and I ask the minister what provision was made to enable those provinces and municipalities to get the money they need for their projects.
Mr. Speaker, I will not conclude my remarks without saying a word or two about a question which is very close to my heart, because I represent, as you know, a constituency with a majority of workers. I should like at this point to talk about the unemployed, a question which the government tried to keep under the carpet, a question which the government tried to prevent us from discussing because it has neglected for the past two or three years to convene the committee on industrial relations, and I say that it is a shame that this very committee should be the only one to remain inactive when the main problem in Canada, the most important

domestic problem is precisely that of unemployment. We have never been told why the committee on industrial relations was not sitting. Since the Prime Minister takes so much pride in the fact that a great number of committees are sitting, I ask him to explain to the house why the committee which perhaps could have made the most important contribution is precisely the one the government did not want to sit?
Mr. Speaker, under this government, the unemployed have been ignored, forgotten, abandoned. Every month, when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) reports on the unemployment situation in Canada, he uses the D.B.S. figures. He does not use the actual figures that he gets from the unemployment insurance commission. He does not give us either a figure that nobody can question: the number of persons now receiving unemployment insurance benefits. The identity of an unemployed and the number of the unemployed people could give rise to all sorts of arguments, but one fact remains undeniable: on April 30 last, 714,894 Canadian citizens were receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that those people are unemployed in a statutory sense, and their number does not include other citizens who have waived their unemployment insurance benefits and whose names do not appear on these lists.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with another matter, and submit that it is a field which comes under the leader of this house. As a matter of fact, it is not the first year that the situation has arisen, I mean that discussion of the labour department estimates is delayed until the last days of the session, probably for the purpose of preventing hon. members from asking the Minister of Labour too many questions. We have the same situation this year. Consequently, I say that the government did, by every means and every possible action, prevent an honest discussion of the unemployment problem in Canada, and I believe that such lack of responsibility with regard to the unemployment situation is the greatest criticism that can be levelled against this government.
Mr. Speaker, I recently asked the minister why the Department of Labour did not call a meeting of Canadian municipalities to give them some information on the winter works program. It is not in the fall that we will be able to interest municipalities in such an undertaking. If the minister told me that the government had greater success this year than last year, I should answer him that he
The Budget-Mr. Drouin is right, but I would add that, if the winter works program had been made known earlier to the municipalities, we might have employed many more men on those projects last winter.
The Minister of Labour has no excuse for delaying information to the municipalities about the program which he intends to submit to the house for next winter, and I hope that the scope of those projects will be broader. I also hope that the government will pay more than 50 per cent of labour costs under that program so that the lot of the jobless can be improved to some degree.
Mr. Speaker, those are the comments I wanted to make in connection with this budget, and in my opinion its impact has been weakened by the fact that it was submitted by the Minister of Finance at a time when the government has obviously lost the confidence of the Canadian people.
The total popular vote in the last four by-elections, gave the Liberal party a majority. The latest Gallup polls also show a majority in favour of the Liberal party.
It therefore seems high time that the Canadian people are due for a change of administration. It is obvious that such a change is eagerly sought at this time and I do hope that the government will soon give us this opportunity which the Canadian people are so anxious to have.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to have this opportunity to give to the house my impressions on the recent budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). He and the government are to be highly commended for their tremendous, magnificent, intelligent, enlightened and detailed work in relation to Canada's economic orientation in the present year.
You will agree, Mr. Speaker, that in a few minutes time, it is impossible to deal fairly with the various aspects and technicalities of the present budget; however, I note that it will benefit every segment of the population and that every economic sector, whatever its level, will enjoy a most satisfactory development brought about by measures which are not artificial but natural and solidly based. Thus the Canadian nation will be assured that its investments have not been left to chance and will not be subjected to the risks of a short and artificial show.
6910	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drouin
In relation to expenses, the figures that make up the various items of the departmental estimates assure us of a brilliant future on the basis of the past year and of spectacular events we have witnessed and which are known throughout the world.
The present government of this great country, through its genius and skill, has managed to breathe new life into the Canadian people and gain the friendship and respect of the world. It would be grossly unfair to take issue with the expenses in the field of external affairs, because this government has been able, through a mixture of intelligence, diplomacy and occasional severity, to gain for Canada the respect and confidence of every nation.
Mr. Speaker, is this not a fact that deserves to be stressed in this house, when nearly half of the world is sitting on a volcano, when most countries are meeting with competition on the markets, when hunger is a permanent feature of certain countries, when whole populations are without shelter, when others roam the deserts and the deepest jungles in search of a shirt or a pair of shoes, when nations are torn by racial strife, when all those countries are faced with such troubles and have to spend much of their national income on armaments and armies, is it not a fact that we in Canada are fortunate to live under the banner of a provident and enlightened government, considering the size and geographic position of the country. This is a country inhabited by two equally great and proud races who live in harmony; we have managed to gain the respect and affection of our powerful neighbours to the north and to the south. While those neighbours talk to each other over our heads, while our friends to the south say certain things about our friends the Cubans and the Peking government, at the same time Canada's external and trade relations are at the highest possible level, and never have Canada's name and goods been so well known.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, in failing to mention in this house a "comparative" situation in which we have been living and are still living at the present time. I submit that the least mistake on the part of the Prime Minister or his Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) would immediately plunge Canada into very difficult circumstances in view of its geographic and highly strategic location. There was nothing that could compare at the time of the Suez incident, because Suez is just a very small spot on the map.


All this goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians can be mighty proud of the government in power. Statistics have proved time and again that no other people in the whole world have more bread, meat and material for clothes and leather for shoes than the Canadian people.
In this country, we hold the world's record in the matter of housing, with every citizen having more cubic feet of living accommodation at his disposal than people anywhere else in the world. We also use more gasoline for touring than do our neighbours to the south.
There, Mr. Speaker, we have a comparative which the opposition has never had the frankness or the courage to admit in this house.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has on several occasions attempted to disparage our country. In referring to Hansard for April 18, I find he claims to be the one who enjoys world confidence, and that it is the Liberal opposition whose statements are believed in other countries. It was Voltaire who said:
Lie, lie; something will always come out of it.
For once Voltaire was mistaken. Of all the opposition's sarcasms, little remains if we consider the enviable position which this country occupies, as a result of this government's energy and vitality.
When opposition members speak in this house they remind me of the devil attempting to preach a sermon. Mr. Speaker, never before has a government shown so much insight and fairness in the distribution of public funds. Citizens at all levels have a share in them.
Never before have so many public works been undertaken; never before have municipalities received so much help and consideration for the promotion of their development; never before, either, have our veterans received better treatment and, there again, never before has a government done so much for the development of a merchant marine and the promotion of shipbuilding in this country. Never before has a government done so much to promote family housing, farm credit, and loans for the recovery of industry in general. And then there is the action taken to encourage the sale of motor cars and the technical training of the unemployed.
A hundred million dollars have been set aside for a survey of the problem of water pollution, a vital problem which so far had been sadly neglected.
We can claim credit for organizing 75 per cent of vocational and technical training. The

Conservative government has shown very special regard for export trade, providing funds for it in amounts never equalled in the past. We have built railroads that have opened new access roads to the development of our national wealth.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that those few remarks will refresh the memory of the opposition. I would like to remind the house that there is an area in the province of Quebec that the government at the time had forgotten. I refer to the constituency of Dorchester which I have the honour of representing in the House of Commons. My constituents are always amazed at the amount of attention they have been getting from a federal government since 1958. Because of its geographical situation the constituency of Dorchester cannot take advantage of certain legislation due to the fact that, like nine out of 10 constituencies in the province of Quebec, it has no adjacent navigable waterways; yet it has benefited from the millions of dollars that have gone to municipalities in the form of public works, subsidies and public buildings. There, Mr. Speaker, is a summary of the activities of a vigorous government, a government that has a sense of responsibility.
I am sure that the people of Canada are quite happy with the new provisions included in this budget, one fully in accord with the political program that the Prime Minister submitted to the people in 1958, and which was endorsed by this nation.
Mr. Speaker, the budget that has been presented to the people of Canada, with a fair balance of fiscal, financial and trade policies, is designed to give fresh impetus to Canada's economy, to develop unused capacity for production, to increase trade and, in this way, to multiply jobs. The result will be increased development of our resources, so that every citizen may get his share of our national economy. That is what this budget holds for the people of Canada. Such is its purpose, a purpose which meets the fondest wishes of the people of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not part of my duties to act as opposition critic of the government on financial and monetary matters. However, I have general remarks to make following the budget speech delivered last Tuesday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
The most striking feature is no doubt the announcement of a deficit of approximately $650 million for the fiscal year 1961-62.
The Budget-Mr. Boulanger
While the new measures resulting from this budget will bring about a tax reduction about $100 million, we are wondering, as do the taxpayers, to what extent the economic activity will be increased if we rely on the experience of past years when we had enormous deficits.
The fact is that our deficit in 1958 was $38.5 million; in 1959, $609.5 million; in 1960, $413 million; in 1961, $345 million; while that for the current year will reach $650 million.
If the figures for the 1962 deficit prove correct, and if we add to them a decrease of about $900 million in the unemployment insurance fund and about $160 million in the national defence fund, we get a total deficit of $3,121 million for the four years of Tory administration.
Can we rely on the figures supplied by the Minister of Finance as to the expected deficit for 1962?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me only one question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall give permission to my hon. friend only when I have concluded my remarks, because I do not think I will be able to say everything I have in mind in the short time at my disposal.
I maintain that we cannot rely on the figures provided by the Minister of Finance since he has never been very good at crystalgazing. Last year, when he introduced his budget, he forecast a $12 million surplus; it all turned out into a $345 million deficit, or a difference of $333 million, that is, a third of a billion dollars.
We are therefore inclined to feel that if the minister makes the same mistake, it is not a $650 million deficit that we will have but a $1 billion deficit, which means a charge of $750 per family.
We had hoped that, after increasing the already enormous debt load which bears down on each Canadian family, the government would have shown itself fatherly and given us the gift it promised us during the 1957 and 1958 electoral campaigns. In fact, here is the promise the Prime Minister made in Toronto and which was reported in the April 29, 1957 edition of Quebec city's he Soleil:
The high taxes party has been in power too long, added Mr. Diefenbaker. The present tax structure practically amounts to confiscation and, if it is allowed to go on like this, it will spell the end

The Budget-Mr. Boulanger of tree enterprise. The leader of the Conservative party does not wish to encourage attempts at tax evasion, but had harsh words for government employees who act as spies and tyrants and who, by their action, infringe upon the rights of Canadians.
Not only has the tax burden not been lightened but it has been made heavier.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you think of the excise tax on automobiles?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What provisions are there in the present budget to help average families?
As the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) just stated, the tax on automobiles has been repealed; it was to be repealed four years ago. Besides, it is not so much the average taxpayer who will benefit from that provision, because the workers cannot afford the luxury of changing their cars every spring. When they can buy a car, they keep it for seven or eight years.
The government has made possible the manufacture of a slightly heavier cigarette.
But what has been done to enable farmers to benefit from their share of the national income of which we heard so much about during the 1957 and 1958 electoral campaigns?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Remember butter at 64 cents a pound.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, I intend to keep on with my speech. If the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has questions to ask, I would ask him to wait until I have concluded my remarks.
The government has changed the excise tax on poultry imported from the United States and reduced the rates on secondary products. That is all.
But there is nothing in the budget to make the average working man enthusiastic.
We now have in power a Tory government which takes after the Bennett government of 1930-35.
During the four years and a half of the latter regime, we had the worst depression in our history. It was truly at the time the rule of poverty and of hunger, of which the soup-ticket was so symbolic.
Today the Tory government is resorting to camouflage and fleeting visions. In years to come it will be nicknamed "The Unemployment Party" or "The no one will suffer Party."

Here again promises galore were made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and also by many candidates in the 1957 and 1958 elections. They were going to put the industry back on its feet.
What a forceful electoral campaign was undertaken in the areas which depend on that industry.
I remember listening to talks on television by Conservative candidates who today are members for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) and for Richmond (Mr. Dubois).
Their enthusiastic line of talk, backed by the dictatorial Union Nationale, gave them victory at the polls. But since then have we heard anything from them about that industry?
I especially remember a vision of the member for Sherbrooke, in a speech, in 1958, full of recommendations to his government.
Since then, the member for Sherbrooke has kept rather silent in this house on that matter of textiles.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has not been a year he did not talk about it.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I intend to submit a few specimens of those releases. I will give only the titles.
In 1958 as reported in La Tribune, the member for Sherbrooke said this:
Ottawa introduces two changes to solve the textile problem.
Of courses, they were nice changes.
September 10, 1958, he said:
Aid from municipalities sought to save the textile industry-
At a time when the member for Sherbrooke was asking municipalities to cut down taxes and grant special rates on electric power, on November 14,	1958, he wrote an article
entitled:
Mr. Allard is preparing a study on textiles.
On November 24, 1958, another spectacular heading:
Seek answer to textile problem.
Nothing yet had been saved.
On December 16, 1959, the press reported:
M.P. asks parliament to inquire into the textile industry. One of the main points, imports.
A few weeks later, that is on January 13, 1960, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated:
Higher Japanese exports welcomed.

On March 20, 1960, another item is entitled:
Mr. Allard endorses any measure that could save the textile industry-
Here is what was stated in June 1960 in a report which appeared in La Presse under the title:
Textile situation calls for moderate optimism.
Naturally, the situation was deteriorating instead of improving. The hon. member for Sherbrooke did recognize it.
Last year, in July 1960, again according to an article reproduced in La Presse, the hon. member for Sherbrooke said:
Ottawa shall have to take action to protect the textile industry.
The situation was not as good as in 1958.
This spring, in March 1961, at the Conservative convention, there was adopted a resolution introduced by Mr. Allard, federal member for Sherbrooke, and seconded by Mr. Andre Langlais, urging the federal government, among other things:
To impose quotas on foreign textiles in the most vulnerable sectors of the Canadian economy.
That is about all the work done by the hon. member for Sherbrooke. After having recognized that the textile industry had been saved, we now hear him say, in 1960 and in 1961, that we must not be overly optimistic about textiles.
Another member, representing St. Hya-cinthe-Bagot, referred on some occasions to textile products.
A few weeks ago, he told us, among other things, that 11 new industries had been set up in St. Hyacinthe since the coming to power of the Conservative government.

His reasoning seems confused. Would he be afraid if he spoke his mind to have a bad reputation as was the case in 1959? We will recall that at that time the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) had said things that had not given satisfaction to a certain textile workers union in the city of St. Hyacinthe. I have here an article published in Le Progres du Saguenay, on October 14, 1960. I quote:
Sales of Japanese textiles and clothing in Canada reached such a volume last year that they represented an expenditure of $2.38 per man, woman and child in the country.
That makes up an astonishing amount, considering that sales of those Japanese products in the United States only represent $1.50 per head, and 30 cents per head in Europe.
If textile imports from Japan do a lot of harm to our Canadian industry, U. S. imports do no less.
I see that I have to summarize my remarks. An article published in the June 1960 issue of the magazine Affaires says this:

Mr. Speaker, this increase in our textile imports from over the southern border is the result of subsidized exports by the United States government. Moreover, it was announced that those subsidies would be increased to a large extent as from August 1, 1961.

In fact it strikes me as strange that the remedies advocated during the 1957 and 1958 elections cannot be applied today.
Has the government lost heart? Yet, it has available a good way, all set and prepared, which lies in the full enforcement of the anti-dumping legislation, which authorizes the Minister of National Revenue to determine the value for excise tax purposes of goods entering this country.

After this great Grosart advertisement of last week, which the Minister of Finance could not conceivably have made up because it was succinct and catchy whereas we know the Minister of Finance and his cold porridge, I knew that this budget was going to be the greatest anticlimax we had ever had in our budgetary history. Whenever you put out this misleading, inflated advertising and then produce the kind of empty package that we got on Tuesday night, you find that the public is let down. This is what happened once again with the present government.
There is another very striking feature about this budget. As I was following the minister in the reading of the budget speech the other night, when he reached page 10 which was about one sixth of the way through that dull, tedious document, I noted the minister had adopted about one third of Mr. Coyne's proposals and I wrote on the margin of my paper, Coyne and water, more water than Coyne. I was surprised to find that I was not the only one who had that reaction. A distinguished member of the press gallery, a particular favourite of the minister's, used exactly the same phrase in his broadcast that same evening, so I am told. I defy any fair-minded person, and when I say that I exclude the Minister of Finance, to go through the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance and find a single item, with one exception, that is not a pale reflection of Mr. Coyne's memorandum. Everything the minister has proposed, not as clearly nor in nearly as good English and certainly not as succinctly or as comprehensively-of course he did not propose a lot of the things in Mr. Coyne's memorandum-is in Mr. Coyne's memorandum.
The one exception is something the minister described only a year ago as a great gamble with the taxpayers' money. The minister said this was dangerous financial speculation. This is the one thing that the minister has produced that Mr. Coyne did not, in some fashion, recommend, and the only thing in this so-called expansion budget. Expansion is undoubtedly the right word, but there is a synonym for that word "expansion",


and the synonym that is generally used in these matters is the word "inflation". We had an inflation of the publicity, and then the air just petered out of the balloon that night as the 58 pages of the budget were slowly, tiresomely and boringly read to this house. The minister steadily lost his audience and several of his colleagues actually slept through it, which perhaps was the best treatment it could have been given. Never before has there been such an anticlimax in our budgetary history. Never before, sir, in any respectable country has a minister of finance erected the fouling of one's own nest into a principle.
It is true that after a war and in other very critical times a few countries have had to depreciate their currencies because they were in dire straits and this was the last possible remedy available. They went from one riding to another. Ministers went into the province of New Brunswick and in the first instance they offered them a cabinet seat, and told the people there that if they did not elect the Conservative candidate they would not have anyone in the cabinet. They came into my riding and offered defence contracts; they went into the riding of Peterborough and they offered contracts there; and they went into the riding of Leeds and offered public works projects. Mr. Speaker, we have in this country a feeling of unrest, and since I have been a member of this house I have heard the responsibility for that charged to a

number of people, and in particular by those who sit opposite the treasury benches. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, and others on the treasury benches, have gone on television and radio and out in the hustings and have told the people of the country that we in the official opposition were the ones that cast doom and gloom and caused the uncertainty and unrest. That was until recently; but now it is claimed1 that the Bank of Canada and its governor caused all this unrest.

Recently it has been suggested that it was the president of the Canadian National Railways who has caused all this uncertainty. I am told that previously it was the chairman of the film board. There have been other persons accused; someone else was always responsible.
Then, if you read the minister's speeches on budgets-which I had occasion to do last night-since he took over his office you will see that he blames the rest of the world. We in Canada are having the greatest government we have ever had. The rest of the world does not seem to appreciate that. In my lifetime, Mr. Speaker, I have been proud of Canada, proud of its reputation around the world for stability and for good government. I am no longer proud.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why is it that the other countries of the world are afraid of Canada? Why is it that when this Minister of Finance makes a speech the Canadian dollar plunges? Why is there chaos in the financial world? Why is it that the private and public corporations of this country are in a state of confusion and anxiety? Why is it that the municipalities of this country are unable to prepare their budgets? Why is it that hon. members of this house are unable to go back to their constituents and say that this is a solid, responsible program? It is because, first, this government delays the budget and then beats the drums so that the people believe there will be real assistance to the economy and then they drop the people.
The municipalities, hydro, the provinces, had to borrow money in the last couple of years outside this country and the Minister of Finance knew it very well. They had to because all of the money in the market in Canada had been sucked up by this government. Now they are left with nothing but a devalued dollar with which to pay this off, and again it is the taxpayers who pay. This Minister of Finance said last year-and it can be seen in black and white-that the dollar would not be devalued. It is a most incredible somersault to find that he can come back to this parliament in a little over a year after saying what he did in the flattest most unequivocal language, which he used in March, 1960. It was obvious then that it could never be contemplated that the Canadian dollar would be devalued by government manipulation. But this minister has come back and unblushingly done it. He has done it to a point where no one knows where it will end. He has not indicated whether it will be 2 cents or 20 cents or just what it is he wants. The people of this country do not know what this government will do because .t has followed, if anything, a policy of lurching from crisis to crisis. It has not in the four years since it has been in office had any plan, any policy. Oh, yes, I remember the Prime Minister said in a speech to Conservatives last fall, which was widely reported, that up until that time the ministers of the crown had been learning their jobs. It might have been better for the country if after three years in which they could not learn their jobs the Prime Minister had tried out some of those other gentlemen to my left.

There is one thing, Mr. Speaker, which has caused this feeling of lack of confidence in this country, and I charge to the government as a deliberate planned proposal, the only one they have had. I refer to a plan originally conceived to keep the opposition in a state of alarm, but with the highly unhappy consequent circumstance of keeping the country in a state of alarm. They have cried "wolf"; they have cried "election". This has happened in respect of every proposal they have brought in, every time there has been a suggestion that it was not a perfect proposal. Every time anything has been put before them the Prime Minister has stood up and wagged his chin, and the Prime Minister's seat mate has stood up and wagged his finger, and they have threatened to take us back to the country. I can only say, Mr. Speaker, "Take us to the country". How gentlemen opposite will then find out what the feeling of the country is-

I am a member of my party. I know they are people of courage, that they have been responsible for a great government and will be again shortly.
Here we are, Mr. Speaker, in a situation where the people do not know where to turn. We are now in June. Last August we had the worst unemployment figures in Canada's history. I prophesy, not as a matter of doom and gloom, that they will be greater still in the coming August and this is a frightening prospect for a country which reaches a condition approaching really full employment-and by that I mean a condition in which no one who wishes to work is out of work-only during the full summer months. We are not able to do anything about our

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis climate. This government has abandoned its right; it has abandoned all the tools which it has to use.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that we had the baby budget, this deformed child, last December, and that following it there was the provision introduced by the Minister of Labour, I believe, to assist areas which were called areas of surplus manpower. That provision was very nearly laughed off the statute books by the people of this country. It was said at that time to be a tremendous assistance for new industry; so tremendous that now in the new budget we have had another proposal of much more major importance to apply all across the country.
Well, perhaps I should not too harshly judge those on the other side. There was a member of the treasury benches

now unhappily no longer a member of this house but of the other place-a former secretary of state, who said in 1959, perhaps in justification for this government's past and future actions, as reported at page 2961 of Hansard: We did all that could be done. Of course, our methods can be questioned .. .
If I understand the rules, Mr. Speaker, it is not proper in this house to question the bona fides, the good intent of hon. members opposite. I cannot question motives but I would expect that every person who has been honoured with a seat in this venerable house, no matter for how short a time, would be a man or woman who had the greatest benefit for Canada at heart. But there are more things necessary than good intentions, Mr. Speaker, and I am told there is a road to a certain place, not the other place, which is paved with them. It is not sufficient to take office and to have good intentions. If this government has given up, if it cannot or if it will not introduce proposals in this house to be of assistance to the country and if it will not do so soon, then I ask that the government and its supporters go back to the country to receive the judgment which they so richly deserve.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to remind the house that a year ago today the province of Quebec escaped from bondage and freed itself from the Duplessis dictatorship. I am glad to point out to the house that the people in Quebec tonight and since last June 23 are finally enjoying freedom under a democratic administration.
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard speeches delivered by opposition members. I have the

privilege of being the third speaker in a row from this side of the house and I am pleased to note that the government side seems to be lacking in fighters. Of course, if I had to come to the defence of the Conservative party and of the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance, I should also be most reluctant to rise in this house. But fortunately, Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on behalf of a riding whose constituents had foreseen, as early as 1958, that it would be a pity to vote for the Conservatives and tonight we note once again, during the discussion on the budget submitted by the Diefenbaker government, through its Minister of Finance, a fourth deplorable deficit in four years of administration.
If the deficit could be explained by important accomplishments on the part of the government, like all other members of this house, I could admit the existence of a deficit. But four deficits without solving any of the present problems, nor any of the problems resulting from a bad Conservative administration since 1957, that is too much.
Mr. Speaker, in order to find years comparable to those we are now going through, we must go back to the years of Borden, Bennett and Diefenbaker-the three BBD years of Canada, Bennett, Borden, Diefenbaker-years of darkness, of carelessness and of decline for this country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the greatest confusion was reigning in the house a while ago; indeed, order has not yet been restored. Not only are the Conservatives unable to stand up in defence of their budget but they constantly interrupt members of the opposition who do their duty in this house. By the way, I would say that they could at least have the decency of listening attentively to a representative of the fair sex. When we, on this side of the house, have the opportunity of hearing a woman from the other side, we listen carefully and respectfully as should always be done towards a woman.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) fortunately succeeded in expressing the views of her constituency and she did her duty when she said that the people of Canada are most deceived with the present administration.
I was speaking of years of confusion. Naturally, that is not the Conservatives' fault. When things go badly, the previous governments are always to blame. When things go wrong, the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) holds the C.B.C.

people, the C.N.R. people or the Bell Telephone people responsible for all the government's wrongdoings. The government is looking for victims right and left; it is Mr. Coyne who is to blame, or Miss Judith Jasmin of the C.B.C., or Mr. Rene Levesque, or Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, or Mr. Donald Gordon. All those heads have to be cut off to prove to the Canadian people that someone is to blame. Well, Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who is a very sympathetic fellow: Stop looking for heads; if you wish the country to prosper, cut one head off, that of your present leader. Vote Liberal at the next election and all problems will be solved.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be a disaster.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking of confusion. In the whole history of our country, have you ever seen a government change its mind so often. The Minister of Finance is always either retracting or contradicting himself. I said a while ago that I did not expect to speak tonight because I thought some of the hon. members opposite would show some fighting spirit. Looking over to the other side, I tried to find traces of this change of mind, this change of opinion, this whirlpool of uncertainty to which we are used and which is characteristic of the Conservatives.
The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) was tried about everywhere: solicitor general, secretary of state, minister of transport.
The minister of transport was shifted to trade and commerce while the minister of trade and commerce (Mr. Churchill) was being transferred to veterans affairs.
The minister of veterans affairs was sent to the Senate.
The same was done with the secretary of state, and for good reasons, he was such a sick man.
As for the minister of agriculture, he was given national defence.
The minister of national defence was sent somewhere else and he is now lieutenant governor in a province.
Then the minister of northern affairs and national resources was moved to agriculture while the minister of agriculture received the national defence portfolio.
There you have the only changes made. There is no mistake about it, the more it changes the more it is the same.
It shows what a wash-out this government has been for the country.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, to shuffle ministers and transfer them from one de-
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis partment to another is no solution to the problem facing this country. The way to settle this problem is not to transfer ministers but to invite members of the opposition to sit to the right of the Speaker and to allow clever men like the hon. members for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and others to play the part that is theirs, and to give to the country the Liberal prosperity which was so appreciated.
Mr. Speaker, for the last three years, even four years, we have been watching the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and hearing him explain his policy.
In 1958, for example, the Minister of Finance was saying that he had just come into the legacy left by the Liberals, that he was new to his post.
He would then explain to the house and the public that it would take time to reorganize his department according to Tory pattern and to put the country back on the road to prosperity.
In 1959, the Minister of Finance comes forward with a deficit. His explanation: it is obvious that we are having a slight recession: but next year, things will be better, finance will be reorganized, the situation balanced and we will present concrete results.
1960, 1961: deficits. But now, the blame is on Mr. Coyne, the fault lies with Judith Jasmin, Rene Levesque, Alphonse Ouimet, Donald Gordon. Even the Bell Telephone is to be blamed, it is a bad company.
If our economy lacks stability, those people are certainly not to blame, but the fault lies with the present Prime Minister who asked the people's trust in the general election campaign of 1958.
He never said that, if elected, he would not be able, because of the persons I just mentioned, to solve the problems in four years. He said: Trust me. I will take the job.
He said: As long as I am Prime Minister, no one will suffer, deficit or no deficit.
Mr. Speaker, tonight we must remind him of his promises. We must tell our friends opposite that people are suffering from unemployment at this very moment.
We have to remind the Prime Minister that he did not fulfil any of his promises.
We are forced to remind the Minister of Finance that he should have organized what is now called his economic expansion pro-

But no, Mr. Speaker. In 1958, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) rose in this house to ask the government to kindly consider the problem of the automobile industry in Canada.
In 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961, the hon. member for Essex East recalled that in his native city of Windsor, as well as in the major cities where cars are being made, there was some slackening in business and unemployment, because the government admitted foreign cars into Canada, and did not protect the Canadian car market.
This government has been aware of that situation for four years-four years during which we have seen the automobile industry going into a slump; four years during which we have seen our car plants laying off thousands of employees, who swelled the numbers of unemployed in Canada.
At that time, the Minister of Finance could find no solution to the problem.
But, feeling that elections are now in the offing, he suddenly finds, after four years of administration, that it might perhaps be wise to listen to and put into practice the suggestions made by the hon. member for Essex East.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the 7.5 per cent tax should be abolished, but unfortunately, it is a bit late to do so.
Now that the automobile industry has laid off a considerable number of workers; that the European car market has been organized on a solid basis throughout the country, it may be a little too late; it would surely have been easier and wiser to put those proposals in effect as soon as they were announced.
What about the pitiful situation of the textile industry in this country?
Not only Liberal members, but even Conservative have, for the last four years, urged the government to adopt economic measures to protect that industry.
What has the Conservative government done? They turned a deaf ear.
There was no known solution, no possible means. We were facing competition against which we could do nothing.
Then, all of a sudden, after four years, the Minister of Finance says he has found means to assist the textile industry, at the very moment it is dying.
I could also, Mr. Speaker, talk about the dollar problems.


While the Minister of Finance said two or three years ago that it was absolutely impossible to devaluate the Canadian dollar, because it would have created a terrible economic chaos, the same Minister of Finance after rejecting that suggestion during four years of administration comes out this year with a broad smile and tells us that it is wise to devaluate the Canadian dollar.
No wonder we are disappointed and that the people of Canada are also disappointed, profoundly disappointed with the budget.
We do not believe the Minister of Finance has the confidence of the people, after making, as he has, year in year out for four years, promises that he has not kept at any time or in any way.
Mr. Speaker, we are now faced with an intolerable situation. Our economic situation is far from being enviable. On the contrary, it deteriorates from day to day.
Therefore, I urge the Minister of Finance to cease claiming he has found the solution to this problem, when he fails to take the necessary steps to do so.
He has brought forward nothing that could help the Canadian economy.
All across the country, people were expecting a general federal election as early as next September.
Mr. Speaker, I am not one of those who entertain this view.
This government is a Tory government, an historically and fundamentally Conservative government.
The Hon. Mr. Borden clung to power as long as he could before being defeated. The Hon. Mr. Bennett extended his years of office as long as he could before being defeated.
This government will do just the same and will extend its administration until March or April 1963, when the people of Canada, after five years of suffering and enduring, will finally free the country from this lame administration that we now have had for four years.
What have you done, my Conservative friends, of those famous public works projects that you announced in all corners of the country? One billion dollars of public works. That was the promise the Prime Minister made everywhere in Canada.
What have you done, hon. gentlemen of the government? Absolutely nothing.
The government say that they want to solve the unemployment problem, but they do nothing to this end.
We, in the opposition, have submitted several suggestions to the government for several years now. Had the government been

serious, they would have listened to us and now, instead of being in an unemployment period, in a period of uncertainty, and instead of experiencing an unhealthy economy, we would have restored the financial situation of this country and we would be living in happier years.
Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for the Conservatives to keep the promises which were made, not only in my constituency, but in Chambly-Rouville and other ridings in that area, to the effect that if they were carried back to power the Richelieu seaway would perhaps be considered.
Now, Mr. Speaker, four years have gone by and the Richelieu is still flowing past our shores. This government has done absolutely nothing in his respect.
Mr. Speaker, as I said and shall repeat every time I rise in this house, the unemployment problem in Canada will never be settled only by long term projects of national scope. The one means for remedying the present unemployment situation, and revitalizing and strengthening our economy, is to solve the problems of each district in the most beneficial way.
To my mind, the Richelieu seaway should have been considered as from 1958; the planning should have been submitted by engineers in 1959 and, in 1960, we should have been able to tell our people: We cannot proceed with the Richelieu seaway, for such and such a reason. On the other hand, if the project had been considered practical, we should have gone ahead and explained to the population why it could be carried out. But no, there again, we have seen the same utter sloth on the part of the government.
The Minister of Transport is still here tonight. I am trying to catch his eye to tell him how much the people of Quebec have been disappointed not only because of the Richelieu seaway, but in almost every field connected with his department. There has been no progress in the field of transport in the province of Quebec, since the present minister took over that department. He did less than nothing. There is a vacuum. The result is naught.
Well, Mr. Speaker, instead of coming to us with statements and promises for our part of the country, the minister should give us what we want, that is serious consideration of the Richelieu seaway. It is his responsibility to do so. And when he comes to the Queen Elizabeth hotel, in Montreal, to tell us that
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis the project will not pay, I shall ask him once again, to prove it in this house and to our people.
Obviously, the minister smiles. It is very funny indeed. He does nothing and smiles. Well, let him smile while there is time, because, after the next general election, our friends will shed crocodile tears when they sit on this side of the house.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) is again interjecting. It is the only thing he can do properly. I should very much like to hear him discuss seriously and objectively the Richelieu waterway. In any event, I think he will have to discuss it with his constituents some day, and I am sure that when he does, four years too late, he will be given an extended leave of absence from the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, I again ask the government to make a study of the Richelieu waterway project. Further, I repeat to the Minister of Finance that deepening the Richelieu is the only way to revitalize our area.
I also urge the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), who lives in our immediate area, to do his share and try to persuade the government to consider this great Richelieu scheme, a scheme which has been seriously considered by the governments of the states of New York and Vermont as well as the United States government. The scheme was also the subject of a serious study on the part of the chambers of commerce, the boards of trade and many well thinking people in our area.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there are those who think that to revitalize the economy of a country, all you have to do is to make statements and promises. There are others who say: When things are bad, you must do as the Roman emperors: give the people bread and games. That is why some ministers of the crown take a lofty attitude with regard to this problem despite the fact that it is close at hand.
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to say to the house that the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance has been a disappointment to the entire Canadian population, because they need action which will yield immediate results.

Today, after four years of depression under a Conservative government, what will be the effect on the Canadian economy of the removal of the 7J per cent excise tax on cars? None whatsoever. A citizen who can afford to buy a car priced at $3,200 will certainly not change his living standard if the price of the car is reduced to $3,000. Four years ago, however, when it was time to act, European cars were allowed to invade the Canadian market, thus contributing to the lay-off of thousands of workers by the Canadian automotive industry. We are now faced with a situation that was entirely created by the Conservative government.
Mr. Speaker, having studied the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, I am trying as you are to find something this government has done for the unemployed. I find not a single thing. What does the present government suggest for the unemployed? Not a single thing.
What solution is this government planning to put forward in the matter of federal-provincial relations? None whatever. What is the Conservative government planning to do to get us out of our difficulties? It calls upon its smiling Minister of Finance to propose a fifth deficit, which will amount to something like $1 billion, and tell the people of Canada: "Let's go into the red, and get around the problem that way".
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada have had enough of the deficits of the Minister of Finance. The people should be used to them because if we take a look at the past, we find that the last four deficits instead of helping the Canadian people have resulted in a shaky and dangerous economic situation. The next deficit will lead to a new period of inflation whose effects will start to be felt a few months hence. Conditions will then be worse than those facing us at this time and the government will say once again: "We were wrong; we thought that the recession was over and that the great Donald had found the solution".
But, again I say, this is a deficit that not only will reach the billion dollar mark, but within a year-and I shall be here to see it-the estimated billion dollar deficit will be $1J if not $2 billion.
Mr. Speaker, with those members in this house who are of good faith, I repeat that the Conservative government has been a failure, and I remain convinced that this government will not call elections in the immediate future. Why? Because public opinion has been tested recently. One test was


held last year and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Clermont) is here as a result. There was a further test last year. The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) is here as a witness. And this year, since the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm asked me, I shall say that the Liberal party, in the last four by-elections, has won four great victories of which we are proud because, first, in the constituency of Leeds, we have taken a stronghold away from the Conservative party.
Second, in Kings riding in Prince Edward Island, the Conservative majority was only 165, while in 1958 they had a majority of 1,134 votes.
In the constituency of Esquimalt-Saanich, the Conservative candidate had a majority of 769 votes, while his predecessor had a majority of 14,000 votes.
In the Restigouche-Madawaska riding, all the big guns of the Union Nationale party had been brought into action, but the victory was only a flop for the Conservatives, since the temporary member for Restigouche-Madawaska only received a majority of 960 votes, while his predecessor had secured a majority of 4,000 votes. The conclusion to be drawn is that the Liberals secured 44 per cent of the popular vote, and the Conservatives, 43 per cent.
Here is another conclusion: in 1958, in the Restigouche-Madawaska riding, the Conservative party had received 60 per cent of the vote, and that percentage is now brought down to 43 per cent, while the Liberals, who had then secured only 32 per cent of the vote, have now overtaken the Conservatives.
Hon. members of the Conservative party, we shall outride you, and soon there will be only three or four of you sitting on this side of the house to the extreme left of Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, may I simply call it 10.30?
